title: Tokio Gives Progress, Not Ordering: Scheduling 1M Tasks
excerpt: How spawning 1M Tokio tasks preserved throughput while letting polling order drift from event submission order, and why task creation needs an application-level bound.
content_html:
This is a prequel to my previous article, Your Rust Service Isn't Leaking — It Could Be the Allocator.

In that post, I wrote about how a few memory allocators behaved differently under our workload. Before we figured out that the memory behavior was tied to allocators, we first tried to reduce the memory usage from the application side.

Our service was event-driven:

  1. Read events from a message queue (Kafka/Redis Streams/NATS)
  2. For each event, spawn a Tokio task to process it

Our Task Pattern

In our workload, each event had a maximum of 1000 user tokens. For every user token, we had to make an outbound call, wait on I/O and collect all responses belonging to the event.

Here is a simplified version of the code where we fan-out tokio tasks for user token, fan-in the responses, and generate a response event.

struct Event { 
    payload: Bytes,  // ~4KB
    user_tokens: Vec<String>, // up to 1000 tokens
    // other fields
}

...
// in main
loop {
    let event: Event = fetch_next_event().await; 

    tokio::spawn(async move {
        let data = event.payload.clone();

        let mut tasks = JoinSet::new();
        for token in &event.user_tokens {
            let token = token.clone();
            let data = data.clone();
            tasks.spawn(async move {
                // hits an outbound API and returns response
                process(token, data).await
            });
        }

        let mut responses = Vec::with_capacity(event.user_tokens.len());
        while let Some(res) = tasks.join_next().await {
            responses.push(res)
        }

        generate_response_event(event, responses);
    });
}

Our primary focus here was throughput. While the fan-out above is unbounded, I assumed it practically wouldn't be a problem. These Tokio tasks are short-lived. They finish and drop once they receive responses, usually within a few milliseconds. So I assumed tasks spawned early would also finish early. Though individual outbound calls could finish out of order, I expected the earlier events overall to finish first, even while newer events were still coming in.

Our requirement was just to make each outbound call as fast as possible so that the burst could finish within the expected time.

What the Logs Looked Like

Here's how our logs looked during a burst of 1000 events, each containing ~1000 user tokens, spawning ~1M tasks in total:

started: event 1, user 5
started: event 1, user 8
started: event 1, user 2
started: event 2, user 6
started: event 2, user 4
started: event 3, user 8

...

finished: event 779
finished: event 976

started: event 900, user 42
started: event 900, user 261
started: event 1, user 974
started: event 1, user 831

...

finished: event 5
finished: event 3

While the burst finished within the expected time, the logs showed that the token tasks from earlier events were being started much later.

I didn't expect strict ordering between tasks. They could complete in any order, and that was fine. What surprised me was how far some of the earlier tasks drifted from their submission order before receiving their first poll.

Inside Tokio's Scheduler

Tokio’s multi-threaded runtime has a fixed number of worker threads, a local queue per worker and a global queue shared across workers. Each worker has a local queue with a capacity of 256 tasks and on overflow it moves half of its tasks to the global queue. Workers prefer pulling from their own local queue first, check the global queue occasionally, and steal from other workers when they are idle.

When the tasks become independently schedulable, Tokio no longer knows which event created them. Now they are just runnable tasks which competing to be polled.

A simplified picture looks like this:

                                global queue
                      +------------------------------+
                      | * overflow from local queues |
                      | * remotely scheduled tasks   |
                      | * mixed older/newer work     |
                      +--------------+---------------+
                                     |
           +-------------------------+-------------------------+
           |                         |                         |
           v                         v                         v
        worker 0                  worker 1                  worker 2
     +-------------+           +-------------+           +-------------+
     | local queue |           | local queue |           | local queue |
     | up to 256   |           | up to 256   |           | up to 256   |
     +------+------+           +------+------+           +------+------+
            |                         |                         |
            v                         v                         v
        poll task                 poll task                 poll task

With this architecture, once our event fans out into 1000 user token tasks, those tasks get mixed with the token tasks from other events, parent event tasks waiting on JoinSet, and tasks waking from I/O readiness.

With so many tasks being submitted at the same time, Tokio does not guarantee that earlier tasks get polled first. Tasks from different events compete for the available worker queues, and scheduling decisions like queue overflow and work stealing can change the order in which tasks are picked up. As a result, some tasks from earlier events received their first poll much later.

The core distinction is:

task created != task polled != task completed

While Tokio continues making progress on every task, memory is affected by how many tasks are live at the same time.

Every Tokio task carries some state and though that state might not be huge individually, when thousands of these tasks are live at the same time, it adds up to the peak memory usage.

And since a few tasks from earlier events in our workload stayed alive till the end of the burst, their parent event tasks also remained alive, keeping the event state in memory, which increased our peak memory usage.

Task Creation Needs a Bound

Tokio guarantees fair scheduling under a bounded number of tasks and assuming no task blocks a worker thread.

Our code had no bound on task creation initially:

read events as fast as possible
  └── spawn one event task per event
        └── spawn up to 1000 token tasks per event

Tokio takes as many tasks as you give it and keeps making progress on them. The boundedness assumed by Tokio for its fairness guarantee has to come from the application.

These bounds vary based on workload. In our case, what we wanted was event-level fairness. We wanted all the token tasks belonging to a single event to be polled and finish closer to their submission time.

To achieve this, we used a Semaphore to bound the number of events that can be processed at a time.

allow only N events into processing at once
  └── spawn one event task per event
        └── spawn up to 1000 token tasks per event

The maximum number of tasks Tokio sees at a time, which affects how fair it can be, also depends on how long each task takes to return on poll. We did some trial-and-error to find the Semaphore count which worked for us.

An important detail here is that even with this bounded structure, the burst finished within the expected time while reducing the peak memory significantly. In general, it might seem that adding a Semaphore would impact the throughput of the service, but that wasn't the case for us.

Not a Tokio Problem

This wasn't a Tokio problem. Even with 1M live tasks, Tokio kept making progress until our burst finished on time. The difference was between my assumption (the event as a whole should finish early if started early) and what the Tokio runtime sees (a task is a task, whichever event it came from).

This was an easy miss for me because there was no correctness issue. There were no tasks which dropped midway or noticeable delays in the service, and our throughput requirements were also met. It just showed up as a higher-than-expected memory spike for reasons that didn't appear anywhere in the application logic.

Conclusion

Spawned early doesn't mean first-polled early. First-polled early doesn't mean completed early.

If there is an application-level unit of fairness you expect Tokio to honor, like the event in our case, the runtime doesn't know it exists. The bounds should be added by the application.

And before spawning a Tokio task, ask what the maximum number of live tasks at a time could be and see how that can impact memory. In some cases, it could also impact other resources which your tasks hold while they are alive.

blocks.html_en: To achieve this, we used a Semaphore to bound the number of events that can be processed at a time.

sentences.en: To achieve this, we used a Semaphore to bound the number of events that can be processed at a time.
sentences.zh: 为了实现这一点，我们使用信号量来限制一次可以处理的事件数量。

blocks.html_en: The maximum number of tasks Tokio sees at a time, which affects how fair it can be, also depends on how long each task takes to return on poll. We did some trial-and-error to find the Semaphore count which worked for us.

sentences.en: The maximum number of tasks Tokio sees at a time, which affects how fair it can be, also depends on how long each task takes to return on poll.
sentences.zh: Tokio 一次看到的最大任务数会影响其公平性，还取决于每个任务返回轮询所需的时间。

sentences.en: We did some trial-and-error to find the Semaphore count which worked for us.
sentences.zh: 我们进行了一些尝试和错误来找到适合我们的信号量计数。

blocks.html_en: An important detail here is that even with this bounded structure, the burst finished within the expected time while reducing the peak memory significantly. In general, it might seem that adding a Semaphore would impact the throughput of the service, but that wasn't the case for us.

sentences.en: An important detail here is that even with this bounded structure, the burst finished within the expected time while reducing the peak memory significantly.
sentences.zh: 这里的一个重要细节是，即使使用这种有界结构，突发也会在预期时间内完成，同时显着减少峰值内存。

sentences.en: In general, it might seem that adding a Semaphore would impact the throughput of the service, but that wasn't the case for us.
sentences.zh: 一般来说，添加信号量似乎会影响服务的吞吐量，但对我们来说情况并非如此。

blocks.html_en: Not a Tokio Problem

sentences.en: Not a Tokio Problem
sentences.zh: 不是东京问题

blocks.html_en: This wasn't a Tokio problem. Even with 1M live tasks, Tokio kept making progress until our burst finished on time. The difference was between my assumption (the event as a whole should finish early if started early) and what the Tokio runtime sees (a task is a task, whichever event it came from).

sentences.en: This wasn't a Tokio problem.
sentences.zh: 这不是东京的问题。

sentences.en: Even with 1M live tasks, Tokio kept making progress until our burst finished on time.
sentences.zh: 即使有 100 万个实时任务，Tokio 仍不断取得进展，直到我们的突发按时完成。

sentences.en: The difference was between my assumption (the event as a whole should finish early if started early) and what the Tokio runtime sees (a task is a task, whichever event it came from).
sentences.zh: 区别在于我的假设（如果提前开始，整个事件应该提前完成）和 Tokio 运行时所看到的（任务就是任务，无论它来自哪个事件）。

blocks.html_en: This was an easy miss for me because there was no correctness issue. There were no tasks which dropped midway or noticeable delays in the service, and our throughput requirements were also met. It just showed up as a higher-than-expected memory spike for reasons that didn't appear anywhere in the application logic.

sentences.en: This was an easy miss for me because there was no correctness issue.
sentences.zh: 这对我来说很容易错过，因为不存在正确性问题。

sentences.en: There were no tasks which dropped midway or noticeable delays in the service, and our throughput requirements were also met.
sentences.zh: 没有出现任何任务中途丢失或服务出现明显延迟的情况，也满足了我们的吞吐量要求。

sentences.en: It just showed up as a higher-than-expected memory spike for reasons that didn't appear anywhere in the application logic.
sentences.zh: 它只是显示为高于预期的内存峰值，其原因在应用程序逻辑中的任何地方都没有出现。

blocks.html_en: Conclusion

sentences.en: Conclusion
sentences.zh: 结论

blocks.html_en: Spawned early doesn't mean first-polled early. First-polled early doesn't mean completed early.

sentences.en: Spawned early doesn't mean first-polled early.
sentences.zh: 早期生成并不意味着早期首次轮询。

sentences.en: First-polled early doesn't mean completed early.
sentences.zh: 尽早首次投票并不意味着提前完成。

blocks.html_en: If there is an application-level unit of fairness you expect Tokio to honor, like the event in our case, the runtime doesn't know it exists. The bounds should be added by the application.

sentences.en: If there is an application-level unit of fairness you expect Tokio to honor, like the event in our case, the runtime doesn't know it exists.
sentences.zh: 如果您希望 Tokio 遵守应用程序级公平性单位（例如我们案例中的事件），则运行时不知道它存在。

sentences.en: The bounds should be added by the application.
sentences.zh: 边界应由应用程序添加。

blocks.html_en: And before spawning a Tokio task, ask what the maximum number of live tasks at a time could be and see how that can impact memory. In some cases, it could also impact other resources which your tasks hold while they are alive.

sentences.en: And before spawning a Tokio task, ask what the maximum number of live tasks at a time could be and see how that can impact memory.
sentences.zh: 在生成 Tokio 任务之前，询问一次实时任务的最大数量是多少，看看这会如何影响内存。

sentences.en: In some cases, it could also impact other resources which your tasks hold while they are alive.
sentences.zh: 在某些情况下，它还可能会影响您的任务在活动期间所拥有的其他资源。

content_html_zh:
这是我上一篇文章《你的 Rust 服务没有泄漏——可能是分配器》的前传。

在那篇文章中，我写了一些内存分配器在我们的工作负载下如何表现不同。 在我们发现内存行为与分配器相关之前，我们首先尝试减少应用程序端的内存使用量。

我们的服务是事件驱动的：

  1. 从消息队列读取事件（Kafka/Redis Streams/NATS）
  2. 对于每个事件，生成一个 Tokio 任务来处理它

我们的任务模式

在我们的工作负载中，每个事件最多有 1000 个用户令牌。 对于每个用户令牌，我们必须进行出站调用、等待 I/O 并收集属于该事件的所有响应。

这是代码的简化版本，我们在其中扇出 tokio 任务以获取用户令牌、扇入响应并生成响应事件。

struct Event { 
    payload: Bytes,  // ~4KB
    user_tokens: Vec<String>, // up to 1000 tokens
    // other fields
}

...
// in main
loop {
    let event: Event = fetch_next_event().await; 

    tokio::spawn(async move {
        let data = event.payload.clone();

        let mut tasks = JoinSet::new();
        for token in &event.user_tokens {
            let token = token.clone();
            let data = data.clone();
            tasks.spawn(async move {
                // hits an outbound API and returns response
                process(token, data).await
            });
        }

        let mut responses = Vec::with_capacity(event.user_tokens.len());
        while let Some(res) = tasks.join_next().await {
            responses.push(res)
        }

        generate_response_event(event, responses);
    });
}

我们这里的主要关注点是吞吐量。 虽然上面的扇出是无限制的，但我认为这实际上不会成为问题。 这些东京任务是短暂的。 一旦收到响应，通常会在几毫秒内完成并丢弃。 所以我假设提前产生的任务也会提前完成。 尽管个别出站呼叫可能会无序完成，但我预计较早的事件总体上会首先完成，即使较新的事件仍在传入。

我们的要求只是尽可能快地拨打每个出站电话，以便突发能够在预期时间内完成。

日志是什么样的

以下是我们的日志在突发 1000 个事件期间的情况，每个事件包含约 1000 个用户令牌，总共产生约 100 万个任务：

started: event 1, user 5
started: event 1, user 8
started: event 1, user 2
started: event 2, user 6
started: event 2, user 4
started: event 3, user 8

...

finished: event 779
finished: event 976

started: event 900, user 42
started: event 900, user 261
started: event 1, user 974
started: event 1, user 831

...

finished: event 5
finished: event 3

虽然突发在预期时间内完成，但日志显示早期事件中的令牌任务的启动时间要晚得多。

我没想到任务之间会有严格的顺序。 他们可以按任何顺序完成，这很好。 令我惊讶的是，一些早期任务在收到第一次民意调查之前偏离了提交顺序。

Tokio 调度程序内部

Tokio 的多线程运行时具有固定数量的工作线程、每个工作线程一个本地队列以及一个在工作线程之间共享的全局队列。 每个工作线程都有一个可容纳 256 个任务的本地队列，并且在溢出时会将一半任务移至全局队列。 Workers 更喜欢先从自己的本地队列中拉取，偶尔检查全局队列，并在其他 Worker 空闲时窃取。

当任务变得可独立调度时，Tokio 不再知道哪个事件创建了它们。 现在它们只是竞争轮询的可运行任务。

简化的图片如下所示：

                                global queue
                      +------------------------------+
                      | * overflow from local queues |
                      | * remotely scheduled tasks   |
                      | * mixed older/newer work     |
                      +--------------+---------------+
                                     |
           +-------------------------+-------------------------+
           |                         |                         |
           v                         v                         v
        worker 0                  worker 1                  worker 2
     +-------------+           +-------------+           +-------------+
     | local queue |           | local queue |           | local queue |
     | up to 256   |           | up to 256   |           | up to 256   |
     +------+------+           +------+------+           +------+------+
            |                         |                         |
            v                         v                         v
        poll task                 poll task                 poll task

使用此架构，一旦我们的事件分散为 1000 个用户令牌任务，这些任务就会与其他事件的令牌任务、等待 JoinSet 的父事件任务以及从 I/O 就绪状态唤醒的任务混合在一起。

由于同时提交如此多的任务，Tokio 不保证较早的任务首先得到轮询。 来自不同事件的任务会竞争可用的工作队列，队列溢出和工作窃取等调度决策可能会更改任务的获取顺序。 因此，早期事件中的一些任务很晚才收到第一次民意调查。

核心区别在于：

task created != task polled != task completed

虽然 Tokio 在每项任务上不断取得进展，但内存会受到同时运行的任务数量的影响。

每个 Tokio 任务都带有一些状态，尽管该状态单独而言可能并不大，但当数千个这样的任务同时运行时，它就会增加内存使用峰值。

由于工作负载中早期事件中的一些任务一直保持活动状态，直到突发结束，因此它们的父事件任务也保持活动状态，将事件状态保留在内存中，这增加了我们的峰值内存使用量。

任务创建需要一个界限

Tokio 保证在有限数量的任务下进行公平调度，并假设没有任务阻塞工作线程。

我们的代码最初对任务创建没有限制：

read events as fast as possible
  └── spawn one event task per event
        └── spawn up to 1000 token tasks per event

Tokio 会承担您分配的所有任务，并不断取得进展。 Tokio 为其公平性保证所假设的边界必须来自于应用程序。

这些界限根据工作负载而变化。 就我们而言，我们想要的是事件级别的公平性。 我们希望对属于单个事件的所有令牌任务进行轮询并在更接近其提交时间时完成。

为了实现这一点，我们使用信号量来限制一次可以处理的事件数量。

allow only N events into processing at once
  └── spawn one event task per event
        └── spawn up to 1000 token tasks per event

Tokio 一次看到的最大任务数会影响其公平性，还取决于每个任务返回轮询所需的时间。 我们进行了一些尝试和错误来找到适合我们的信号量计数。

这里的一个重要细节是，即使使用这种有界结构，突发也会在预期时间内完成，同时显着减少峰值内存。 一般来说，添加信号量似乎会影响服务的吞吐量，但对我们来说情况并非如此。

不是东京问题

这不是东京的问题。 即使有 100 万个实时任务，Tokio 仍不断取得进展，直到我们的突发按时完成。 区别在于我的假设（如果提前开始，整个事件应该提前完成）和 Tokio 运行时所看到的（任务就是任务，无论它来自哪个事件）。

这对我来说很容易错过，因为不存在正确性问题。 没有出现任何任务中途丢失或服务出现明显延迟的情况，也满足了我们的吞吐量要求。 它只是显示为高于预期的内存峰值，其原因在应用程序逻辑中的任何地方都没有出现。

结论

早期生成并不意味着早期首次轮询。 尽早首次投票并不意味着提前完成。

如果您希望 Tokio 遵守应用程序级公平性单位（例如我们案例中的事件），则运行时不知道它存在。 边界应由应用程序添加。

在生成 Tokio 任务之前，询问一次实时任务的最大数量是多少，看看这会如何影响内存。 在某些情况下，它还可能会影响您的任务在活动期间所拥有的其他资源。
